scores.evidence: Every client edits locally and all copies converge. The server relays and saves edits but does not decide between them
scores.rationale: Claims about Yjs/CRDT behavior, state-vector resync, OT fallback, and durability semantics are accurate, and the plan states real limits (encoded-size overhead of deleted text, GC tuning, server cannot reject individual edits).

scores.evidence: Several users edit the same document at once, see each other's changes live, and every document is saved permanently
scores.rationale: Covers live co-editing, persistence, sharing, presence and version history with explicit, justified deferrals and realistic sequencing, but never mentions undo (a core editor capability) and version history is view-only with restore unaddressed.

scores.evidence: The server writes the edit to the Postgres edit log before confirming it. Peers receive the edit right away
scores.rationale: Responsibilities and data ownership are clear (API vs collaboration server vs Postgres), and decisions like save-before-confirm, workspace-ID seam, and schema versioning are honored consistently across budgets, phases and validation.

scores.evidence: Property-based fuzz test: 2–10 simulated clients doing random text, formatting and structure edits, 10,000 seeded runs nightly
scores.rationale: Each risky decision has a named validation (V1 convergence before format commit, V3 chaos before real content, V5 before exposure), thresholds are labeled assumptions, and production checks (drift detector, synthetic two-client probe, SLO) continue after launch.

scores.evidence: ASSUMPTION: a commonly cited point where edits feel live; product owner to confirm
scores.rationale: Every number is labeled ASSUMPTION or UNKNOWN with an owner to confirm it, and the 'Missing inputs' section states exactly which assumptions would change the phase order and how.

scores.evidence: Chaos test: 20 bot editors for 30 min, kill -9 the collaboration server about every 2 min, one managed database failover
scores.rationale: Covers the hard domain failures concretely: silent divergence (drift detector), lost confirmed edits, compaction corruption (replay comparison), live-session permission bypass, forged/revoked tokens, hostile pasted HTML, flooding, Redis and login-provider outages.

scores.evidence: A deploy and a rollback both succeed through the pipeline. Killing the database connection fires the save-failure alert
scores.rationale: Deploy/rollback, add-only then add-then-remove migrations, connection draining, restore drills, meaningful alerts, runbooks and an on-call load review are all specified and explicitly sized to a 4–8 person team.

scores.evidence: Hosting cost per connection is recorded at the Phase 4 exit.
scores.rationale: Identifies the drivers (connections/hosting, on-call people cost), has concrete controls (editor caps, flood limits) and a build-vs-buy trade-off, but gives no order-of-magnitude estimates for build or run cost, deferring everything to measurement.

scores.evidence: R3: the saved format and sync protocol depend on it; once real documents exist, switching means converting every document
scores.rationale: Explicitly classifies each decision's reversibility, validates the one-way choices (merge model, saved format, IDs, tenancy) before data becomes permanent, keeps data disposable until V3, and names exit paths including a tested export.

scores.evidence: One codebase, two deployables (HTTP API and WebSocket collaboration server), one Postgres
scores.rationale: Starts with the minimum viable topology, adds Redis and multi-server only after V4 proves the need, defers offline, search, export and E2EE with named triggers, and omits nothing essential to correctness or security.

scores.evidence: If copies differ: fix or report upstream, else switch to server-ordered edits (OT). If too slow: tune Yjs garbage collection or split documents
scores.rationale: Phases have dependency-justified ordering, specific tasks, checkable exit criteria, and every validation states what it unlocks and the concrete fallback if it fails, so a team could start immediately.

checklist.evidence: Merge-by-design shared data type (CRDT: Yjs + y-prosemirror)... Do not build our own merge engine
Minimal ProseMirror schema v1 (paragraphs, headings, lists, bold/italic/link). Every snapshot is stamped with its schema and format version
converges under concurrent, cut-off, reordered and duplicated delivery... 10,000 seeded runs nightly
Compact the edit log into snapshots: decode each snapshot and compare it with a replay of the log before deleting log entries
several servers sharing edits through Redis (Hocuspocus Redis extension)... Cap editors per document and slow down senders who flood it
Survive short disconnects only (unsent edits buffered in memory, resync on reconnect)
Checked on the server when a connection opens and on every edit (viewers' edits rejected). Revoking access disconnects live sessions
version-history view built from the snapshots
live cursors and presence (temporary, never saved)
Phase 1: Convergence, document model, identity... Then the lower-risk features, each one schema-evolved through the V2 suite
Benchmark on a 1 MB document with a simulated year of history... p95 < 200 ms, p99 < 500 ms at 50 editors
a v1 and a v2 client on one document. The v2 client adds a new kind of content (node or mark); the old client edits around it

traps.evidence: Every client edits locally and all copies converge
Do not build our own merge engine, and do not use a hosted collaboration vendor
An allow-listed staff member signs in, creates a document, and types "hello". A second browser session sees it
The server writes the edit to the Postgres edit log before confirming it
Yjs converges for this schema and is fast enough at the target document size [ASSUMPTION... Validated by V1]

note: An exceptionally rigorous, correctly sequenced CRDT-based plan with labeled assumptions and risk-first validation; its only notable gaps are collaborative undo/restore semantics and the absence of any cost estimates.
